main.title: Detective Comics #27
main.summary: Detective Comics #27 is an American comic book of the Detective Comics anthology series, which debuted the superhero Batman in a featured story called "The Case of the Chemical Syndicate" during the Golden Age of Comic Books.

cards.heading: Detective Comics #27
cards.text: Detective Comics #27 is an American comic book of the Detective Comics anthology series, which debuted the superhero Batman in a featured story called "The Case of the Chemical Syndicate" during the Golden Age of Comic Books. It is considered one of the most important and valuable first appearance debuts from DC Comics alongside Action Comics #1, released the previous year. In addition to the debut of Batman, Detective Comics #27 included several other stories featuring established and original characters. These features represented the range of genres covered by the anthology series at the time, including crime, espionage, western, and mystery fiction.

main.title: Fantasia
main.summary: Fantasia is a 1940 American animated anthology film produced by Walt Disney Productions.

cards.heading: Fantasia
cards.text:
Fantasia is a 1940 American animated anthology film produced by Walt Disney Productions. The third Disney animated feature film, it consists of eight animated segments set to pieces of classical music conducted by Leopold Stokowski, seven of which are performed by the Philadelphia Orchestra. Music critic and composer Deems Taylor acts as the film's Master of Ceremonies who introduces each segment in live-action. The film's production was supervised by Walt Disney and Ben Sharpsteen, with story direction by Joe Grant and Dick Huemer. 

Disney conceived the project in 1938 during the completion of The Sorcerer's Apprentice, which was originally planned as an elaborate Silly Symphony cartoon to revive the declining popularity of Mickey Mouse. When rising production costs threatened to outpace the short's potential revenue, Disney expanded the concept into a feature-length musical compilation with Stokowski and Taylor as collaborators. To accommodate the ambitious soundtrack, Disney and RCA developed Fantasound, a pioneering sound system that made Fantasia the first commercial film released in stereo and a precursor to surround sound.

main.title: Hattie McDaniel wins an Academy Award
main.subtitle: The first Black performer to receive a competitive Oscar
main.summary: On 29 February 1940, Hattie McDaniel won the supporting-actress Oscar for her performance as Mammy in Gone with the Wind. She became the first Black person nominated for and awarded a competitive Academy Award. The recognition came at the 12th ceremony, held at the Ambassador Hotel's Cocoanut Grove in Los Angeles, in an industry and a city still organised around racial exclusion.

cards.heading: A first at the Oscars
cards.text: On 29 February 1940, Hattie McDaniel won the supporting-actress Oscar for her performance as Mammy in Gone with the Wind. She became the first Black person nominated for and awarded a competitive Academy Award. The recognition came at the 12th ceremony, held at the Ambassador Hotel's Cocoanut Grove in Los Angeles, in an industry and a city still organised around racial exclusion.

cards.heading: Recognition inside segregation
cards.text: McDaniel had worked on stage, radio and screen, bringing experience as a singer, comedian and actress to roles that Hollywood often confined to domestic service. Her performance in Gone with the Wind made Mammy's reactions and authority an important part of the household scenes. The award recognised that work, but the ceremony exposed the limits of the welcome: McDaniel and her guest were seated separately from the film's other nominees in the segregated venue.

cards.heading: The history of the award
cards.text: Supporting performers then received an engraved plaque. McDaniel later bequeathed hers to Howard University, where it was displayed before disappearing from view. In 2023, the Academy and Academy Museum announced a replacement for the university. That continuing history gives the 1940 award a significance beyond one evening. It records a major professional achievement alongside the unequal conditions under which the achievement had to be made and publicly celebrated.

main.title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
main.summary: The Empire of Japan launched a surprise military attack on the US Pacific Fleet at its naval base at Pearl Harbor in Oahu, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941.

cards.heading: Attack on Pearl Harbor
cards.text:
The Empire of Japan launched a surprise military attack on the US Pacific Fleet at its naval base at Pearl Harbor in Oahu, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941. At the time, the US was a neutral country in World War II. The air raid on Pearl Harbor, which was launched from aircraft carriers, prompted the US to declare war on Japan the next day. The Japanese military leadership referred to the attack as the Hawaii Operation and Operation AI, and as Operation Z during its planning.

The attack on Pearl Harbor was preceded by months of negotiations between the US and Japan over the future of the Pacific. Japanese demands included that the US end its sanctions against Japan, cease aiding China in the Second Sino-Japanese War, and allow Japan access to the resources of the Dutch East Indies. Japan dispatched its naval attack group on November 26, 1941, just before receiving the Hull note, which stated the US desire that Japan withdraw from China and French Indochina.

main.title: Citizen Kane
main.summary: Orson Welles made his feature-film debut with Citizen Kane in 1941, directing, producing and starring in a portrait of media magnate Charles Foster Kane.

cards.heading: Citizen Kane
cards.text: Orson Welles made his feature-film debut with Citizen Kane in 1941, directing, producing and starring in a portrait of media magnate Charles Foster Kane. He wrote the screenplay with Herman J. Mankiewicz, drawing on powerful American businessmen and elements of their own lives. RKO had offered Welles unusual creative freedom after his theatre work and The War of the Worlds radio broadcast. He could develop the story, choose his collaborators and retain final cut. That independence shaped a film concerned with the life and legacy of a powerful public figure.

main.title: Z3
main.summary: The Z3 was a German electromechanical computer designed by Konrad Zuse in 1938, and completed in 1941.

cards.heading: Z3
cards.text:
The Z3 was a German electromechanical computer designed by Konrad Zuse in 1938, and completed in 1941. It was the world's first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer. The Z3 was built with 2,600 relays, implementing a 22-bit word length that operated at a clock frequency of about 5–10 Hz. Program code was stored on punched film. Initial values were entered manually.

The Z3 was completed in Berlin in 1941. It was not considered vital, so it was never put into everyday operation. Based on the work of the German aerodynamics engineer Hans Georg Küssner (known for the Küssner effect), a "Program to Compute a Complex Matrix" was written and used to solve wing flutter problems. Zuse asked the German government for funding to replace the relays with fully electronic switches, but funding was denied during World War II since such development was deemed "not war-important".

main.title: Casablanca
main.subtitle: Rick must choose what to do when Ilsa returns
main.summary: Michael Curtiz's Casablanca sets a love story inside a wartime transit city where refugees hope to find a route out of occupied Europe. Humphrey Bogart plays Rick Blaine, an American café owner whose guarded life changes when Ilsa Lund arrives with resistance leader Victor Laszlo. The film first opened in New York on 26 November 1942.

cards.heading: A city on the way to somewhere else
cards.text: Michael Curtiz's Casablanca sets a love story inside a wartime transit city where refugees hope to find a route out of occupied Europe. Humphrey Bogart plays Rick Blaine, an American café owner whose guarded life changes when Ilsa Lund arrives with resistance leader Victor Laszlo. The film first opened in New York on 26 November 1942.

cards.heading: The room where lives meet
cards.text: Rick's café brings gamblers, officials, refugees and informers into the same rooms. Passages to safety depend on papers, money and favours, making apparently casual conversations matters of consequence. Ilsa's return reveals an earlier relationship in Paris and gives Rick a personal stake in Laszlo's escape. Bogart and Ingrid Bergman's scenes leave much of that history in looks and pauses. The business of the café continues around them, so their reunion never becomes detached from the war outside.

cards.heading: Memory and commitment
cards.text: Songs help connect private memory to public commitment. Sam's performance of As Time Goes By recalls Rick and Ilsa's Paris, while the confrontation between competing songs in the café turns its customers into a visible community. Max Steiner's score draws those musical materials into the drama. Rick's eventual decision gives the romance its lasting shape: the question is what he will do with his influence when the happiness he wants and the help another person needs no longer coincide.

main.title: Colossus computer
main.summary: Colossus was a set of computers developed by British codebreakers in the years 1943–1945 to help in the cryptanalysis of the Lorenz cipher.

cards.heading: Colossus computer
cards.text:
Colossus was a set of computers developed by British codebreakers in the years 1943–1945 to help in the cryptanalysis of the Lorenz cipher. Colossus used thermionic valves (vacuum tubes) to perform Boolean and counting operations. Colossus is regarded as the world's first programmable, electronic, digital computer. The first electromechanical computer was Konrad Zuse's Z3, completed in Berlin in 1941.

Colossus was designed by General Post Office (GPO) research telephone engineer Tommy Flowers, based on plans developed by mathematician Max Newman at the Government Code and Cypher School at Bletchley Park.

Alan Turing's use of probability in cryptanalysis contributed to its design. His earlier electromechanical Bombe addressed Enigma, while Flowers' Colossus worked on the Lorenz cipher.

main.title: Normandy landings
main.summary: Allied forces landed in Normandy on 6 June 1944, opening the invasion of occupied Western Europe.

cards.heading: Normandy landings
cards.text: Allied forces landed in Normandy on 6 June 1944, opening the invasion of occupied Western Europe. Airborne operations accompanied the seaborne assault, codenamed Operation Neptune within the wider Operation Overlord. Planning had begun in 1943, supported by a deception campaign intended to conceal the landing's location and date from Germany. Weather forced a day's postponement, with tides, moonlight and timing limiting the available alternatives. The operation began the liberation of France and helped establish the conditions for Allied victory on the Western Front.

main.title: Harvard Mark I
main.summary: The Harvard Mark I, or IBM Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator (ASCC), was one of the earliest general-purpose electromechanical computers used in the war effort during the last part of World War II.

cards.heading: Harvard Mark I
cards.text:
The Harvard Mark I, or IBM Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator (ASCC), was one of the earliest general-purpose electromechanical computers used in the war effort during the last part of World War II.

One of the first programs to run on the Mark I was initiated on 29 March 1944 by John von Neumann. At that time, von Neumann was working on the Manhattan Project, and needed to determine whether implosion was a viable choice to detonate the atomic bomb that would be used a year later. The Mark I also computed and printed mathematical tables, which had been the initial goal of British inventor Charles Babbage for his analytical engine in 1837.

According to Edmund Berkeley, the operators of the Mark I often called the machine "Bessy, the Bessel engine", after Bessel functions.
